document.title: Ninive (Nineveh)

references.notes: 83-1-18, AH 83-1-18 (mainly BM 74684-77218). Five cases. Dispatch inventory, 18 October 1882: P 5206. There were three cases from Assyria, one from Babylonia, and one mixed. In registration, the intention seems to have been that the bare number 83-1-18 should be applied to the Assyrian material; this was ignored when entries above 83-1-18, 699, were written, and they include some Babylonian objects. The prefix AH, applied to the remainder, created an ambiguity: much of the material no doubt did come from Abu Habbah (especially from the December 1882 consignment, since there were only 850 “very small pieces of inscribed clay” from Abu Habbah in the January 1883 consignment), but there is no reason to suppose that it all did. In practice the AH 83-1-18 tablets sometimes do have A.H. marked on them, and sometimes do not; the initials may sometimes have been put on together with the date-number as a serious indication of provenance, at the time cases were being unpacked, but may sometimes have been added years later as part of the total registration number. Since it was normal for the registrars, or at least Pinches, to rely on these marks when making entries in the provenance columns, we may conclude that AH 83-1-18 tablets which do not have an Abu Habbah provenance in the register-whatever may be written on them now-may have come from the other sites represented in this consignment, namely Babylon and Borsippa. This collection, as registered, contains about twice as many tablets or tablet fragments as were received in the consignment, and there are the usual strays: at least two are entered as coming from Kuyunjik, AH 83-1-18, 1456, 2398 (BM 76091, 77023), and there is one, AH 83-1-18, 1340 (BM 75978), registered as from Abu Habbah though it bears no A.H., which joins a “Dailem” fragment, 82-3-23, 1687 (BM 50695).
